rationale: A wins because it stays closer to the supplied facts and labels the missing proof before a reporter can use it as a knife. "When Your Company Goes Global but Your Corporate Card Doesn't" is a real buyer-led angle and admits it collapses without a named finance lead. B has better teeth in places, but "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" imports payroll and mid-size companies from nowhere. That is not strategy; that is a confident hallucination wearing a blazer.
gaps_in_A: "Corporate Cards Were a US Startup Story. Now the Software Is Going Everywhere." overstates category history; the update says Brex serves venture-backed startups, not that corporate cards were a US startup story.
"historically been the incumbent advantage" is plausible, but not supplied. It needs third-party market context before it becomes a claim.
"dealing with local reimbursement delays, FX friction, and employee complaints" turns likely pain into stated fact. Keep it as a hypothesis until a customer says it.
"Brex's 50-Country Push Is Also a $12.3 Billion Bet" is useful but thin without revenue, burn, or margin context; A notices the hole, but the angle lives or dies there.
gaps_in_B: "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" is wrong-category invention. The update is about corporate cards, expense management, and reimbursements, not payroll or mid-size companies.
"Brex bets 50 countries is the thing Ramp can't copy quickly" invents Ramp's difficulty and Brex's strategic intent. The facts only say Brex competes with Ramp.
"distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer" is unsupported and sweeping. No remote-work, hiring, Series B, or employer-distribution fact appears in the update.
"after years of fighting over the same US venture-backed customer base" smuggles in rivalry history not provided. A reporter may know it, but this exercise did not give it to you.
